rows.speaker: Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī
rows.claim: Farāhī's tract exposes distortions and interpolations and restores the histories of Abraham and the other celebrated figure discussed with him.
rows.anchor: my mentor Ḥamīd al-Dīn Farāhī has exposed all these distortions and interpolations and revived the history of both these celebrated personalities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi found no reliable account of Idrīs in Jewish scripture or Bible history and dismisses earlier exegetical accounts as conjecture.
rows.anchor: All that our past exegetes have written about him is based on conjecture and thus it is useless to cite it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an's mention suggests Idrīs appeared in scriptures known to the People of the Book, while true and false stories circulated about him.
rows.anchor: he was mentioned in the scriptures of the People of the Book and all kinds of true and false stories circulated about him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He offers two possibilities: Arabicized prophetic names obscured Idrīs's name, or an early Torah mention disappeared from later copies.
rows.anchor: the name of Idr īs cannot be recognized

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated loss and oral redaction of the Torah produced discrepancies among copies and continual additions and deletions.
rows.anchor: the Torah vanished a number of times and was written a number of times through its oral redaction.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi regards Idrīs's story as lost Torah content recovered by the Qur'an, which restores the prophet's true history.
rows.anchor: the case of Idr īs (sws) is one of these lost episodes recovered by the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idrīs's character is presented as an example for all mankind.
rows.anchor: His character too was an example for entire mankind.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an praises Idrīs as ṣiddīq, using the same wording by which it praises Abraham.
rows.anchor: He has been praised in exactly the same words as Abraham (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idrīs must have attained this upright status after enduring many trials.
rows.anchor: Idrīs (sws) would have gained this status after passing through may trials.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like Ishmael, Idrīs is regarded as steadfast; the two are also paired in Qur'an 21:85.
rows.anchor: He too has been regarded as steadfast like

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophets' shared perseverance through difficult trials explains their close similarity and Idrīs's lofty rank as a reward.
rows.anchor: Both had to pass through tough trials in which they showed perseverance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an addresses Arab idolaters and People of the Book who claimed descent from the prophets and saw those prophetic lineages as sources of guidance.
rows.anchor: whether they were the Idolaters of Arabia or the People of the Book – all of them ascribed themselves to one of these prophets.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophetic accounts express sorrow that these claimed heirs distorted the religion taught by Abraham, Jacob, Moses, and Jesus.
rows.anchor: they had distorted and disfigured the religion of these celebrated prophets.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophets' prostration and weeping at revelation sarcastically contrasts with their followers' arrogant denial and mockery of the Qur'an.
rows.anchor: they would fall down in prostration while crying is a sarcastic comment on these followers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalaf here means unworthy successors.
rows.anchor: The word ﺧَﻠۡﻒٌ here means “unworthy successors.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi distinguishes the two forms of khalaf, saying the latter is not used positively.
rows.anchor: The difference between ﺧَﻠۡـﻒٌ and ﻒٌ ﺧَﻠَ is that the latter is not used in the positive sense.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inheritance from prophets depends on following their guidance, not on family lineage.
rows.anchor: ascription to prophets and being their inheritors is not something that relates to lineage and family.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer, when properly performed, reminds a person of the covenant with the Lord.
rows.anchor: the prayer if it is offered in the right way which reminds a person of the covenant he has made with his Lord.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Neglecting prayer leaves a person vulnerable to Satan's lures.
rows.anchor: If it is forsaken, it is certain that a person will succumb to the lures of Satan.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi refers readers to al-Baqarah, Āl-i ʿImrān, and al-Anʿām for details of how idolaters and the People of the Book treated prayer, avoiding repetition here.
rows.anchor: Details of what the Idolaters and the People of the Book did with this basic directive of religion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the prophetic teachings pair prayer with zakāh, the verse says successors followed desires rather than explicitly neglecting zakāh; Islahi identifies desire as what blocks charity and spending for God.
rows.anchor: it is not stated that they squandered the prayer and the zakāh; it is stated that they squandered the prayer and followed their desires.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To meet one's deviation means to face its consequence in the Hereafter, reaping what one sowed without injustice.
rows.anchor: they will meet their deviance actually means that they will encounter the consequence of their deviance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised fate is certain to be met by every person, so no one should doubt it.
rows.anchor: the promised fate mentioned will necessarily be met by every person. No one should have any doubt about it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the next world, opposition to truth and its bearers will cease; people will hear no foolish talk, greet one another, and receive angels' congratulations.
rows.anchor: People will not hear any foolish talk there. They will merrily greet one another. Angels too will congratulate the dwellers of Paradise.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Morning and evening refer to Paradise's own realities, which will become clear only there.
rows.anchor: obviously refers to the mornings and evenings of Paradise, the reality of which will only become evident there.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers' sustenance is seeing God and receiving His attention and affection.
rows.anchor: the sustenance referred to her for the believers will be that they will be able to see God and earn His attention and affection.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic usage can call God's blessings and favors sustenance, a sense also found in other scriptures.
rows.anchor: see, for example verse 37 of Sūrah Āl-i ‘Imrān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only servants who keep God's limits inherit Paradise; a claim to Paradise alone does not secure entry.
rows.anchor: not every person who claims to go to Paradise will actually go there. Only they will go there who abide by the limits of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse sarcastically rebukes people who dismantled God's religion yet still claimed they would enter Paradise.
rows.anchor: a sarcastic remark on those who had totally routed God’s religion but still staked a claim for Paradise.
